group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 62-year-old man arrived at the hospital from his own residence after four days of progressive shortness of breath, a cough that turned from dry to purulent overnight, shaking chills, and right-sided chest discomfort exacerbated by deep inspiration. He drove himself in after noticing that walking up the single flight of stairs in his split-level home left him breathless, a change from his usual baseline of being able to mow the lawn without stopping. His medical background includes an ischemic cardiomyopathy with a most recent outpatient echocardiogram six months earlier showing a left-ventricular ejection fraction of 30 %, and a lacunar infarct five years ago that resolved without residual weakness but left him on daily antiplatelet therapy; he follows in a heart-failure clinic every three months and performs his own activities of daily living. He denies any chronic kidney problems, chronic liver disorders, malignancy, or residence in a long-term care facility, and he has not been hospitalized in the past year. Daily medications before today consisted of carvedilol, losartan, furosemide 20 mg, atorvastatin, and clopidogrel. He has no drug allergies. He quit smoking two decades earlier after a 15-pack-year exposure and drinks only one or two beers on weekends; recreational drugs are denied. He received this season’s influenza vaccine at a pharmacy three weeks ago and has not taken antibiotics during the current illness. On arrival he was sitting upright on the stretcher, conversant and oriented to person, place, date, and current events, answering questions appropriately with no slurred speech or confusion. Triage vitals obtained before any antipyretic, intravenous fluid, or antimicrobial therapy showed an oral temperature of 38.4 °C, pulse 93 beats per minute with a regular rhythm, blood pressure 124/78 mm Hg in the right arm, respiratory rate 31 breaths per minute with mild supraclavicular retractions, and oxygen saturation 89 % on ambient air, improving to 92 % when he was asked to sit forward. Skin examination revealed warm, well-perfused extremities without cyanosis or edema. Jugular venous pulsation was just at the level of the sternal angle at 45°, similar to his baseline clinic examinations. Cardiac auscultation disclosed a regular rate and rhythm with a soft S3 consistent with known systolic dysfunction but no murmurs or pericardial rub. Lungs exhibited diminished breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the right posterior lower third with fine crackles above that area; breath sounds were vesicular elsewhere and no wheezes were heard. Abdomen was soft, nontender, and without hepatosplenomegaly. There was no peripheral edema, and distal pulses were intact. Cranial nerves II–XII were intact, strength was 5/5 diffusely, and pronator drift was absent, consistent with his usual post-stroke exam as documented by neurology. Point-of-care capillary glucose measured 120 mg/dL. Laboratory studies drawn within 15 minutes of arrival, prior to any intravenous medications or fluids, revealed a venous blood gas pH of 7.42 with bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, serum sodium 141 mEq/L, potassium 3.9 mEq/L, chloride 102 mEq/L, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 25 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL (unchanged from baseline), and hematocrit 47 %. A complete blood count showed leukocytes 14.8 × 10⁹/L with 88 % segmented neutrophils and platelets 210 × 10⁹/L. An arterial blood gas on room air demonstrated PaO₂ 74 mm Hg, PaCO₂ 38 mm Hg, and corroborated the venous pH. High-sensitivity troponin was negative. Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm at 92 beats per minute with longstanding Q waves in the inferior leads but no acute ischemic changes. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained before any treatment displayed a right lower-lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and a small meniscus of fluid layering posteriorly along the costophrenic angle, consistent with an associated pleural collection; cardiac silhouette appeared unchanged from prior imaging and pulmonary vasculature was not congested. Point-of-care thoracic ultrasonography performed by the emergency physician confirmed an anechoic stripe less than 1 cm in depth overlying the right hemidiaphragm. Blood cultures, sputum Gram stain, and a respiratory pathogen panel were sent before any antibiotics were started. At the moment the admitting team evaluated him, he had received no diuretics, bronchodilators, supplemental oxygen beyond room air for arterial sampling, or antimicrobial agents, and his hemodynamics remained stable with a warm periphery, brisk capillary refill, and no change in mental status.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points at presentation.
- Demographics: a man's baseline score is his age in years (+62). He lives at home, so nursing-home residence adds 0.
- Comorbidities: heart failure with EF 30% (+10) and cerebrovascular disease from a prior lacunar infarct (+10). No malignancy, liver disease, or renal disease (+0 each).
- Examination: respiratory rate 31/min meets the ≥30 threshold (+20). He is oriented, SBP 124 is not <90 mm Hg, temperature 38.4°C is neither <35 nor ≥40°C, and pulse 93 is <125/min (+0 each).
- Laboratory and oxygenation findings: pH 7.42 is not <7.35; BUN 25 is <30 mg/dL; sodium 141 is not <130 mEq/L; glucose 120 is <250 mg/dL; hematocrit 47% is not <30% (+0 each). Using the available room-air arterial measurement, PaO₂ 74 mm Hg does not meet the <60 mm Hg criterion (+0).
- Imaging: a pleural effusion is present, even though small (+10).
Sum: 62 + 10 + 10 + 20 + 10 = 112.
Final answer: 112
